The `fixture` package is the theme's sample API reference: enough symbols to exercise the sidebar, the page, and the source links.

It is not a real library. The [guide](../) explains what the fixture is for.

symbols.name: widget
symbols.docs:
A small widget model used to exercise the renderer.

- `Widget` holds the value.
- `Widget.Config` holds the knobs.
- `render` turns a widget into a string.

## What is not here

No allocator, no threading, no I/O. The fixture exists to make the template's shapes visible, not to do work.

symbols.name: Widget
symbols.signature: pub const Widget = struct { name: []const u8, count: u8 }
symbols.docs: A value with a name and a count. Both fields are public, so `widget.name` and `widget.count` are the whole interface.

symbols.name: init
symbols.docs: Builds a widget with `count` set to zero. The name is borrowed; the caller keeps it alive.

symbols.name: append
Config
symbols.signature: pub const Config = struct { pretty: bool, indent: u8 }
symbols.docs: The options `render` reads. Defaults are in `Widget.Config.default`.

symbols.name: render
symbols.signature: pub fn render(w: Widget, options: Options) []const u8
symbols.docs: Renders a widget into the caller's buffer. The result is a view, not an allocation; see [Zig](https://ziglang.org/) for the language this sample pretends to be written in.

symbols.name: Options
symbols.signature: pub const Options = struct { pretty: bool, indent: u8 }
symbols.docs: Knobs for `render`. The fields mirror `Widget.Config` so a caller can pass either shape.

symbols.name: pretty
symbols.docs: When true, `render` puts each field on its own line.

symbols.name: VERSION
symbols.docs: The fixture version. It changes only when the sample does.
